literature.title: Self-Adjusting Long-Term Medications: A Qualitative Descriptive Study of Patients’ Practices
literature.what_it_means: Small descriptive interview study. Country, payer and patient characteristics are not reported, so transfer to Medicaid members is unclear. It describes reasons for self-adjustment but tests no intervention. The themes may inform how pharmacists frame medication reviews, but it is not enough to change practice.

literature.title: Woebot for Postpartum Mood and Anxiety: Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Feasibility, Acceptability, and Preliminary Efficacy of a Mobile Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Intervention
literature.what_it_means: Pilot RCT with a waitlist control and self-reported outcomes. The efficacy signal is weak (d=-0.16, n=97 symptomatic), and the improvement in stress was exploratory. The sample was mostly White, recruited through a research platform, and payer was not reported, so the Medicaid postpartum transfer is unproven. Engagement was modest, a median of 9 days.

literature.title: Personalizing digital mental health: a micro-randomized trial analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy/dialectical behavioral therapy text messages to improve mood
literature.what_it_means: The design is relevant to Compass message timing, but average effects were null. The moderator findings come from multiple subgroup tests and were not replicated. The sample was mostly highly educated White women from social media, not Medicaid members. Waymark's own heterogeneous-effect rankings failed to validate out of sample.

literature.title: Outpatient Antibiotic Fills and 30-Day Readmission Following Patient-Directed Discharge in Drug Use-Associated Infective Endocarditis in a National Medicaid Cohort
literature.venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
literature.what_it_means: This Medicaid study identifies a high-risk subgroup: patients with drug use-associated endocarditis who leave via patient-directed discharge. Few filled antibiotics within three days. Early fills were associated with lower readmission, but residual confounding, including possible healthy-adherer bias, means the study does not prove that outreach would cut readmissions.

literature.title: Use of digital health tools to promote equitable and efficient health-related social needs screening and response
literature.venue: Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care
literature.what_it_means: This review discusses digital tools for pediatric social-needs screening and referral. The abstract reports no new comparative outcome estimates. It is relevant to Waymark's screening and SMS navigation work; its trauma-informed privacy guidance may inform design, but the abstract does not establish improved outcomes.

literature.title: Skill-guided agentic reasoning enables longitudinal synthesis of myeloma records at expert-level concordance
literature.what_it_means: The main benchmark used myeloma records, not a Medicaid population. For Anchor, the safety lesson is that similar error rates can mask a higher share of clinically significant errors. Adding the skill library also improved iterative RAG. The study evaluated existing records, included exploratory cross-dataset testing, and provides no evidence on patient outcomes.

literature.title: Feasibility of Implementing a Pharmacist-Integrated Collaborative Model for Opioid Use Disorder: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
literature.what_it_means: A single-arm pre-post feasibility study at four sites with no control and no significance testing. The adherence and retention changes are tiny and noisy, and the total sample size isn't reported. MOUD patients are heavily Medicaid, so the topic is relevant, but the study shows feasibility, not effectiveness.

published_findings.title: Comparing Alternative Approaches to Care Management Prioritization: A Prospective Comparative Cohort Study of Acute Care Utilization and Equity Among Medicaid Beneficiaries
published_findings.headline: Targeting care management by predicted benefit beats targeting by risk
published_findings.finding: Prioritizing Medicaid outreach by predicted benefit, rather than predicted risk, was associated with 92 fewer acute care visits per thousand member-months, with similar engagement rates.
published_findings.why_surprising: Risk-based targeting prioritizes patients most likely to need acute care. In this study, targeting Medicaid patients by predicted benefit instead was associated with fewer acute care visits, while outreach and engagement rates were similar.

published_findings.title: Treatment-Effect-Based Versus Risk-Based Targeting of Care Management Outreach in Medicaid: A Retrospective Cohort Study with Machine Learning
published_findings.headline: Targeting by predicted treatment effect prevents about 5x more acute events
published_findings.finding: At the same outreach capacity, allocating care-management calls by predicted treatment effect was estimated to prevent 5.3 times as many acute events as allocating by risk (95% CI 4.9 to 5.7), without widening group disparities.
published_findings.why_surprising: Care-management programs conventionally target high-risk patients, assuming those at greatest risk benefit most. This study found that patients most likely to benefit from outreach differ markedly from those at highest risk, and that matching individuals to outreach based on responsiveness rather than risk yielded substantially better outcomes.

published_findings.title: Preventing tomorrow's high-cost claims: the rising-risk patient opportunity in Medicaid
published_findings.venue: The American journal of managed care
published_findings.headline: Rising-risk Medicaid patients show greater spending growth in a cohort analysis
published_findings.finding: Spending for rising-risk Medicaid patients nearly doubled over the year while spending for high-cost claimants fell 41.6% as costs regressed to the mean; half of new high-cost claimants had been flagged as rising risk.
published_findings.why_surprising: In this observational analysis, high-cost status was often temporary, consistent with regression to the mean. Rising-risk patients' spending grew, suggesting a potential focus for outreach. The analysis does not establish that targeting them prevents disease progression or lowers costs.

published_findings.title: The Risk Of Perpetuating Health Disparities Through Cost-Effectiveness Analyses
published_findings.headline: Cost-effectiveness analyses may systematically disadvantage minority groups
published_findings.finding: Standard cost-effectiveness approaches can make interventions for marginalized groups appear less cost-effective than for advantaged groups by incorporating assumptions that perpetuate existing health inequities, such as differences in baseline costs and competing risks.
published_findings.why_surprising: Cost-effectiveness analysis is intended as a neutral policy tool. Yet standard methods embed structural inequities—like baseline health care costs and insurance status—that make interventions targeting disadvantaged populations look worse on paper, even when addressing greater health needs.

published_findings.title: Clinical decision support for population health management: development and validation of integrated acuity and intervention prediction models
published_findings.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
published_findings.headline: Integrated decision support flags acute care risk before it shows up in claims
published_findings.finding: Integrated prediction model achieved 81.3% sensitivity and 82.1% specificity for 30-day acute care prediction, with 1.59 percentage point absolute risk reduction compared with standard care.
published_findings.why_surprising: Physicians typically make sound clinical decisions, but they relied heavily on recent utilization patterns (75.8% of variance) while models integrated broader signals to identify intervention needs earlier. The modest but consistent risk reduction shows models complement rather than replace clinical judgment.

published_findings.title: Prediction of non emergent acute care utilization and cost among patients receiving Medicaid
published_findings.headline: Medicaid risk model linked to better detection and reversal of racial sensitivity gap
published_findings.finding: In a cohort study, the best-performing model had roughly triple the sensitivity of the standard model (11.3% vs 3.4%) at similar specificity, and reversed the standard model's lower sensitivity for Black versus White patients.
published_findings.why_surprising: The study supports improved Medicaid risk prediction using an alternative modeling approach after data-quality and social-risk data initiatives. It does not establish that collecting richer social risk data alone caused the improvement.

published_findings.title: Medicare Advantage and Type 2 Diabetes Outcomes
published_findings.headline: Medicare Advantage not linked to better diabetes outcomes than original Medicare
published_findings.finding: Among adults with type 2 diabetes, Medicare Advantage was not associated with better hemoglobin A1c, blood pressure, cholesterol, food insecurity, housing instability, or transportation barriers compared with original Medicare.
published_findings.why_surprising: Medicare Advantage can offer financial protections and supplemental benefits, such as healthy food assistance, that might improve diabetes outcomes and address social needs. Yet this cohort study found no evidence of better measured clinical outcomes or fewer social needs than original Medicare.

published_findings.title: Opportunistic Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Using Routine Head CT in the Emergency Department
published_findings.venue: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
published_findings.headline: Routine emergency head CT scans reveal hidden cardiovascular risk
published_findings.finding: Deep learning on routine emergency head CT scans added to traditional risk factors for predicting cardiovascular events, flagging subclinical disease in younger patients with favorable risk profiles.
published_findings.why_surprising: Head CT is not designed for cardiac risk assessment. In this retrospective cohort, deep learning extracted cardiovascular risk information from these scans that complemented traditional risk factors, identifying subclinical disease in younger patients with favorable risk profiles.

published_findings.title: Transferring healthcare risk prediction models between Medicaid populations: a transfer learning evaluation
published_findings.headline: Simple model transfer shows similar discrimination to a complex ensemble
published_findings.finding: A basic transfer approach achieved similar discrimination as a sophisticated meta-ensemble when predicting acute care utilization across Medicaid populations, with recalibration substantially improving calibration.
published_findings.why_surprising: Despite their complexity, advanced methods did not clearly outperform simple transfer on discrimination in this evaluation. Source-only transfer had similar discrimination to the meta-ensemble, but this does not establish equal performance overall. Target-adapted models had smaller fairness disparities, and broader validation is needed.

published_findings.title: Early detection of high risk pregnancies using clinical and social data to improve health outcomes
published_findings.headline: Adding social data to pregnancy risk models boosts sensitivity by 10 points
published_findings.finding: In this Medicaid cohort, adding social data, especially health care access, increased model sensitivity from 71.3% to 81.3%. The augmented model had 94.3% specificity and eliminated the sensitivity gap between Black and White patients.
published_findings.why_surprising: The link between social determinants and maternal outcomes is well established. This study shows their practical value for risk prediction: adding social data improved sensitivity and eliminated the Black–White sensitivity gap in this cohort. It does not establish broader reductions in algorithmic bias or improved health outcomes.

published_findings.title: Offline reinforcement learning for care management: addressing sparse rewards, temporal dependencies, and fairness in Medicaid populations
published_findings.headline: Doubly robust evaluation is associated with more stable Medicaid policy assessment
published_findings.finding: In this Medicaid cohort, standard off-policy evaluation had 0% effective sample size versus 44.2% for doubly robust evaluation. Fairness-constrained training was associated with racial/ethnic intervention disparities of 0.8 versus 3.5 percentage points.
published_findings.why_surprising: High-dimensional action spaces can make off-policy evaluation unreliable. In this Medicaid cohort, doubly robust evaluation was associated with greater stability, while fairness-constrained training was associated with smaller racial/ethnic intervention disparities.

published_findings.title: Redesigning Medicaid frailty algorithms: improved identification of medically frail adults under community engagement
published_findings.headline: Redesigned frailty algorithm identifies 45% more disabled Medicaid adults
published_findings.finding: Existing state algorithms identified mean 31.4% of functionally disabled Medicaid adults as medically frail. A redesigned algorithm incorporating expanded diagnostics increased identification to 45.6%, narrowing racial disparities by 10-46%.
published_findings.why_surprising: States use widely varying thresholds for frailty exemptions despite serving similar populations. A standardized, evidence-based approach substantially improves identification across all states and reduces racial and rural-urban gaps.

published_findings.title: Integrating healthcare system context to improve risk prediction and assess racial disparities among dual-eligible Medicare-Medicaid beneficiaries: a retrospective cohort study using national fee-for-service claims
published_findings.headline: System context reshapes spending risk differently by race
published_findings.finding: Adding healthcare system context to risk models reduced predicted spending for 86% of dual-eligible beneficiaries (mean 8.8 percentage points), but increased it for 14%. Black beneficiaries experienced higher contextual risk amplification (15.8% vs 13.6% White).
published_findings.why_surprising: Risk models typically focus on individual health factors. This finds that system-level factors like care coordination and workforce substantially reshape predictions—and reveals these factors affect racial groups differently, suggesting current models may mask important disparities.

published_findings.title: Medicaid Managed Care Procurement Reveals Systematic Overemphasis of Technology and Equity Performance Claims Across 32 States
published_findings.venue: Inquiry : a journal of medical care organization, provision and financing
published_findings.headline: Medicaid insurers overemphasize trendy topics in contracts, downplay chronic disease care
published_findings.finding: Managed care organizations made 54 times more technology claims and 22 times more health equity claims than state requirements, while underemphasizing chronic disease management and workforce development.
published_findings.why_surprising: You might expect insurance companies to focus contract promises on areas states explicitly require. Instead, they systematically emphasize politically popular topics like technology and equity while de-emphasizing unglamorous but essential services like managing diabetes. This reveals a gap between what sounds good and what actually improves care.

published_findings.title: AI safety evaluation in an underrepresented population: real-world performance of clinical decision support and frontier language models on Medicaid patient messaging triage
published_findings.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
published_findings.headline: Evaluated AI tools fell short of autonomous triage targets in Medicaid messaging
published_findings.finding: No AI tool or combination achieved both 0.80 sensitivity and specificity for autonomous triage. Best balanced ensemble reached 0.69 sensitivity and 0.58 specificity; highest specificity had only 0.30 sensitivity.
published_findings.why_surprising: Medicaid messages had lower reading levels and more colloquialisms than physician-scripted scenarios. No evaluated AI configuration met both accuracy targets for autonomous triage in this cohort, although two configurations met the sensitivity-floor target with clinician review of flagged messages.

published_findings.title: Association of Multidisciplinary Care Team Engagement With Hemoglobin A1c Among Medicaid Enrollees With Diabetes: A Doubly Robust Machine Learning Analysis
published_findings.headline: Care team engagement linked to larger A1c declines with worse baseline control
published_findings.finding: Among Medicaid enrollees with diabetes, care team engagement was associated with a 0.30 percentage point A1c reduction. The estimated association was larger at higher baseline A1c, approaching 1 percentage point among those with baseline A1c ≥9%.
published_findings.why_surprising: The modest overall association masks a larger estimated association among people with baseline A1c ≥9%. This suggests targeted outreach to Medicaid enrollees with uncontrolled diabetes may be worth prioritizing, but the observational study does not establish that engagement caused the improvement.

published_findings.title: Quantifying Indirect Billing Within the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule
published_findings.headline: About 39% of clinician office visits are billed under physicians' names
published_findings.finding: Advanced practice clinicians provided a substantial share of Medicare office visits, and 38.9% of their office encounters were billed indirectly under physicians, hiding who delivers the care.
published_findings.why_surprising: While indirect billing is permitted under Medicare rules, the magnitude is notable: APCs provide substantial care yet bill under physician names at rates varying widely by specialty (about 30% in surgery vs. 4% in primary care), suggesting billing patterns may reflect business practices more than clinical necessity.

published_findings.title: Procedural Prescription Denials and Risk of Acute Care Utilization and Spending Among Medicaid Patients
published_findings.headline: Some prescription denials cost Medicaid more than they save
published_findings.finding: Some procedural prescription denials were associated with more emergency visits and hospital stays, with acute care costs that outweighed the short-term drug savings.
published_findings.why_surprising: Prescription denials aim to curb drug spending, yet denials in some medication classes were associated with higher acute care use and net spending after accounting for drug savings. This observational study does not establish that denials caused those increases.

published_findings.title: Prevalence and Geographic Variation of Serious Mental Illness Among Young Adults Enrolled in Medicaid in New York State
published_findings.venue: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine
published_findings.headline: Homelessness carries the highest odds of serious mental illness in young adults
published_findings.finding: Among young adults enrolled in Medicaid, homelessness (odds ratio 5.49), disability, female sex and rural residence were associated with higher odds of serious mental illness.
published_findings.why_surprising: Asian, Black and Latinx enrollees had lower odds of serious mental illness than White enrollees. This cross-sectional study cannot determine whether those differences reflect underlying illness, diagnosis or other factors.

published_findings.title: Predicting quality measure completion among 14 million low-income patients enrolled in medicaid
published_findings.headline: Clinical data alone predicts Medicaid quality gaps better than random outreach
published_findings.finding: A model using clinical data improved accuracy by 32.5 percentage points over non-predictive methods like alphabetical calling. Adding social determinants data improved accuracy to 84.5% and reduced racial disparities in predictions.
published_findings.why_surprising: Most outreach to low-income patients uses simple methods like birthday reminders or alphabetical calling. This shows that even basic predictive models dramatically outperform these approaches, and that social data further narrows racial prediction gaps—an outcome targeting typically fails to achieve.

published_findings.title: Medicaid Expansion Among Nonelderly Adults and Cardiovascular Disease: Efficiency Vs. Equity
published_findings.headline: Medicaid expansion associated with fewer heart attacks and strokes
published_findings.finding: A simulation model linked Medicaid expansion to fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths among nonelderly adults, with the largest projected gains for lower-income, Black and Hispanic adults; estimates were uncertain.
published_findings.why_surprising: The model suggested that health gains favored lower-income groups, but the economic and equity conclusions were uncertain. Expansion was both cost-effective and equity-enhancing in only 26–29% of probabilistic sensitivity-analysis simulations.

published_findings.title: Reinforcement Learning to Prevent Acute Care Events Among Medicaid Populations: Mixed Methods Study
published_findings.headline: Reinforcement-learning-guided care management linked to fewer acute events
published_findings.finding: Counterfactual analyses estimated that reinforcement-learning-guided care management could yield a 20.7% relative reduction in acute care events versus standard practice among Medicaid beneficiaries (estimated number needed to treat 8.3).
published_findings.why_surprising: Care managers rely on experience and judgment to prioritize interventions. This study suggests that an algorithm trained on patient trajectories could recommend better next steps than standard practice, with counterfactual analyses also suggesting smaller disparities across demographic groups.

published_findings.title: Simulating A/B testing versus SMART designs for LLM-driven patient engagement to close preventive care gaps
published_findings.headline: SMART outperforms A/B testing on cost-effectiveness in outreach simulations
published_findings.finding: In simulations comparing designs for testing personalized outreach, SMART showed better cost-effectiveness and net benefit across all scenarios, with superior power for detecting heterogeneous treatment effects in later stages.
published_findings.why_surprising: Traditional A/B testing compares two alternative messages. In these simulations, SMART offered better cost-effectiveness and net benefit across all scenarios, but its advantage in detecting heterogeneous treatment effects appeared only in later randomization stages.

published_findings.title: Preferences for food vouchers among adults with low incomes
published_findings.headline: Low-income adults prefer unrestricted food vouchers over produce-only options
published_findings.finding: Participants preferred vouchers eligible for all foods over produce-only vouchers, and monthly over weekly redemption. Preferences differed by assignment: those assigned produce-only vouchers were more likely to prefer that type.
published_findings.why_surprising: Flexibility was a key driver of preference, with participants favoring all-food vouchers overall. However, those assigned produce-only vouchers were more likely to prefer that type, showing that preferences differed with participants’ program experience.

published_findings.title: Impact of Vietnam-era G.I. Bill eligibility on later-life blood pressure distribution: evidence from the Vietnam draft lottery natural experiment
published_findings.headline: G.I. Bill eligibility lowered blood pressure at higher quantiles
published_findings.finding: G.I. Bill eligibility, proxied by draft-lottery eligibility, shifted blood pressure toward lower risk: systolic pressure was 3 mmHg lower at the 90th percentile. Protective effects appeared among men with low and medium childhood socioeconomic status.
published_findings.why_surprising: Education subsidies target academic opportunity, not health directly. This natural experiment found larger blood-pressure benefits at higher quantiles, rather than uniform benefits across the distribution. Effects also differed by childhood socioeconomic status, with opposite effects among men in the highest-status group.

published_findings.title: Comparison of Self and Caregiver Reports of Antiretroviral Treatment Adherence among Children and Adolescents Living with HIV in Western Kenya
published_findings.venue: Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care
published_findings.headline: Child and caregiver HIV adherence reports show similarly weak links to pill cap data
published_findings.finding: Child and caregiver self-reports had similarly weak correlations with pill cap adherence measures (0.23 and 0.20, respectively). Both reported fewer missed doses than indicated by the cap data.
published_findings.why_surprising: Caregivers might be expected to report adherence more accurately. In this study, both reports correlated weakly with pill cap measures, suggesting similar reporting limitations. However, this does not establish equal accuracy, and pill caps do not verify medication ingestion.

published_findings.title: Association of Adequacy of Broadband Internet Service With Access to Primary Care in the Veterans Health Administration Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic
published_findings.headline: Better broadband access associated with more virtual primary care visits
published_findings.finding: Veterans with optimal broadband had more video primary care visits and fewer in-person visits after the pandemic began than those with inadequate broadband.
published_findings.why_surprising: One might expect broadband access to simply enable telemedicine as an additional option without reducing in-person care. This shows that better broadband availability was associated with a meaningful shift away from in-person visits, raising questions about whether virtual care fully substitutes for or complements in-person primary care.

published_findings.title: Catastrophic Spending On Insulin In The United States, 2017-18
published_findings.headline: One in seven insulin users face catastrophic out-of-pocket costs
published_findings.finding: Among Americans using insulin, 14.1% spent more than 40% of postsubsistence family income on insulin annually. Catastrophic spending was 61% less likely among Medicaid than Medicare beneficiaries.
published_findings.why_surprising: Insurance coverage does not guarantee protection from high insulin costs. In this cross-sectional study, Medicaid coverage was associated with less catastrophic spending than Medicare coverage, suggesting that coverage type may matter alongside income.

published_findings.title: The Underuse of Medicare's Prevention and Coordination Codes in Primary Care : A Cross-Sectional and Modeling Study
published_findings.headline: Primary care doctors bill for prevention services to only 2% of eligible patients
published_findings.finding: Median billing code use was 2.3% among eligible patients, even though doctors provided appropriate services to 5-61% of eligible patients. If doctors billed half of eligible patients, annual revenue could increase by $124k for prevention and $86k for coordination services.
published_findings.why_surprising: One might expect that if Medicare added billing codes to support primary care, doctors would readily use them to capture available revenue. Instead, most forgo substantial annual income—potentially over $200k per practice—by not billing for services they already provide, suggesting barriers beyond code availability.

published_findings.title: How the Gender Wage Gap for Primary Care Physicians Differs by Compensation Approach : A Microsimulation Study
published_findings.headline: Risk-adjusting pay for patient age and sex narrows primary care physician gender wage gap
published_findings.finding: Female PCPs earned 21% less than male PCPs under productivity-based pay. The gap narrowed to a nonsignificant difference under capitation risk-adjusted for patient age and sex, compared to larger gaps under other risk-adjustment approaches.
published_findings.why_surprising: Female PCPs see younger, healthier, and more Medicaid-insured patients—factors that reduce revenue under most payment models. Counterintuitively, accounting for patient sex in risk adjustment (along with age) substantially closes the gap, suggesting common risk models miss a key driver of compensation differences.
